newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa's Telkom sees profitable future.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa's Telkom sees profitable future.

text.p: South African state communications utility Telkom on Thursday predicted a profitable future as it gains expertise from its international partners and rolls out an ambitious line connection programme.

The firm, 30 percent owned by a U.S-Malaysian consortium, posted a 61 percent jump in annual attributable profit to 1.9 billion rand ($420 million) as revenue rose 23 percent to 16.3 billion rand in the year to the end of March.

Telkom chairman Dikgang Moseneke told a news conference that the current year would also see profit growth, although a six billion rand capital expenditure programme may mean it does not hit the same heights.
The firm's chief financial officer Nor Hizam Hashim said profit growth would remain more than 10 percent. "We will still continue to maintain double digit growth," he said.
Earlier this year -- in a landmark move for South Africa's privatisation programme -- a 30 percent stake in Telkom was sold to a consortium of US-based SBC Communications and Telekom Malaysia.
Moseneke said the benefits of the international link-up were already coming through in terms of technology transfers and the acquiring of international skills and techniques.
"The people are here and they are in place, in our management and we are ready to go," he said.
Telkom said it had beaten an internal target of connecting 250,000 new lines in the past year by almost 6,500. In the process it linked up 95 communities that previously had no phone connection.
In the current year the firm is aiming for more than 350,000 new lines, with at least 256,000 in underserviced areas. It could also hook up more than a 100 new communities.
"It will certainly be in excess of the 95 we connected this year," Moseneke said.
The firm is aiming to create a modernised, digital and nationwide network in preparation for the entry of competition into its market in four years.

Telkom wants to roll-out 2.8 million new lines before 2001 and have a fully digital network by 2002 at the latest. "We are facing competition in four years and we are preparing ourselves," Moseneke said.

The company also aims to strip out unnecessary costs and expects its partners' international experience to help. "We are striving for and will continue to find internal operational efficiencies," Moseneke said.
One problem the firm has faced is theft of its copper wiring as organised crime gangs -- some operating from within the company -- plunder the valuable metal.
Last year there were almost 4,300 thefts, costing the company 230 million rand. Police responded with 433 arrests and disciplinary action was taken against 81 Telkom workers.
Moseneke said the firm was combatting the problem by security patrols of key backbone networks, increasing use of fibre optics and seeking to investigate criminal gangs working among its staff.
"This is something that has dogged us for quite some time...(but) as and when we reduce copper in our network there will be a gradual decline (in theft)," he said.($ = 4.526 South African Rand)
